item.title: NCT deal signed amid protests, police action
item.description:
Bangladesh has signed a 15-year agreement with Dubai-based DP World to operate one of Chittagong Port’s most important container terminals, pushing ahead with a controversial plan that had previously been suspended amid opposition from workers and political parties.
The agreement for the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT), which handles nearly half of the port’s container traffic, was signed on Thursday afternoon at the Invest Bangladesh office in Agargaon, Dhaka, even as protesters gathered outside and police used batons to disperse demonstrators.
The decision marks a significant policy shift for the BNP government, whose leaders had opposed handing over the terminal to a foreign operator during the interim administration.
While the government says the agreement will modernize port operations, attract investment and improve Bangladesh’s trade competitiveness, workers and opposition groups have questioned its financial terms, transparency and implications for national control over strategic infrastructure.
The controversy intensified immediately after the signing, with Chittagong Port labour organizations announcing a daylong mass hunger strike for October 12 and warning of further programs, including action that could bring port operations to a standstill.
Later on Thursday, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman met a DP World delegation led by its board chairman, Essa Kazim, and urged the company to explore further investments in Bangladesh, including free trade zones and rail-based inland container depots.
Under the agreement, DP World will operate and maintain the NCT for 15 years, with an option to extend the arrangement by another 15 years through mutual consent.
Shipping Minister Sheikh Rabiul Alam said the company would invest $150 million, equivalent to approximately Tk1,500 crore, to modernize the terminal.
Bangladesh would also receive Tk600 crore as a signing fee, while the government would retain 67% of the revenue generated under the arrangement, he said.
The minister also referred to an annual payment of Tk10 crore to the port, although the precise relationship between this payment and the broader revenue-sharing arrangement requires clarification.
The terminal, built in 2007 at a cost of approximately Tk2,000 crore, has five jetties and is among the country’s most strategically important container-handling facilities.
The government maintains that ownership of the terminal is not being transferred.
“Leasing out a port and container handling are not the same thing. Those claiming the port is being leased out are unaware of the details of this agreement,” Rabiul Alam told journalists.
He said ownership, security and overall regulatory control would remain with the Chittagong Port Authority and relevant government agencies, including Customs, intelligence and security authorities.
DP World would be responsible for terminal operations, equipment maintenance and technological upgrades.
The government expects the arrangement to improve container-handling efficiency, reduce vessel waiting times and strengthen the country’s import-export infrastructure.
Police disperse protesters with batons during a demonstration against the DP World-NCT deal in Dhaka`s Agargaon on Thursday.
However, the complete agreement, including detailed financial, operational and security provisions, has not been provided in the source material.
The decision carries particular political significance because the proposal has passed through three successive administrations.
Discussions about appointing an international operator began in 2019 during the Awami League government.
In March 2023, approval in principle was granted to pursue an international operator under a public-private partnership arrangement.
The initiative was revived during the interim government, which sought to finalize an agreement with DP World.
But protests, strikes and resistance from port workers forced the authorities to suspend the process ahead of the February 2026 national election.
At that time, BNP leaders in Chittagong opposed the proposed agreement, arguing that an interim administration lacked the mandate to make such a long-term decision involving a strategically important national asset.
After assuming office, however, the BNP government reopened negotiations.
On October 1, the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs gave in-principle approval to the proposed 15-year arrangement.
The agreement was finalized just a week later.
Asked about the government’s change of position, Shipping Minister Rabiul Alam said previous administrations had failed to negotiate terms sufficiently favourable to Bangladesh.
He said the current government had spent six months bargaining with DP World and securing what it considered better conditions.
“We have spent the last six months working on the areas where bargaining was necessary to secure our interests, and we have successfully reached a conclusion. This is an achievement of this elected government,” he said.
The minister argued that the agreement would protect Bangladesh’s interests while bringing international expertise and investment into the port.
The signing took place against a backdrop of demonstrations in both Dhaka and Chittagong.
Activists from the Communist Party of Bangladesh, Bangladesh Samajtantrik Dal and other left-wing organisations gathered outside the Invest Bangladesh office in Agargaon on Thursday afternoon.
They demanded cancellation of the agreement and raised concerns about foreign management of a strategic national facility.
Police dispersed the demonstrators around 2:45pm, shortly before the signing ceremony.
Protesters alleged that police used batons without provocation, injuring several activists, including leaders of the Communist Party of Bangladesh.
CPB President Sazzad Zahir Chandan said the demonstrators had been holding a peaceful program.
“We were holding a peaceful program. At one point, police baton-charged us without any provocation,” he alleged.
He said the parties would continue protesting against what they considered a threat to Bangladesh’s control over its ports and national resources.
Police offered a different explanation.
Sher-e-Bangla Nagar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Monir Hossain told UNB that demonstrators had lain down on the road and obstructed traffic.
“Police removed them for the sake of vehicular movement,” he said.
The protesters’ allegations concerning injuries and the circumstances of the police action could not be independently established from the available accounts.
Police disperse protesters with batons during a demonstration against the DP World-NCT deal in Dhaka`s Agargaon on Thursday. Photo Dhaka Tribune
In Chittagong, labour organizations brought out a procession and held a rally in the port area shortly after the agreement was signed.
They announced a daylong mass hunger strike outside the port building on October 12, demanding cancellation of the deal.
Leaders warned that more extensive protests, potentially disrupting port operations, would follow if the government refused to reconsider its decision.
Humayun Kabir, coordinator of the Chittagong Bandar Rakkha Sangram Parishad, described the NCT as the heart of Chittagong Port.
He argued that a strategically important and functioning terminal should remain under Bangladeshi management.
Speaking to BBC Bangla before the signing, he questioned whether bringing in a foreign operator would increase costs through additional payments and commissions.
He also argued that Bangladesh could modernize the terminal by training existing workers rather than transferring its operation to an international company.
Workers have staged demonstrations, hunger strikes and other programs over several months.
The latest agreement has therefore not ended the dispute but shifted it into a new phase, with opponents now demanding cancellation of a signed contract.
Job security remains one of the principal concerns raised by port employees.
Shipping Minister Rabiul Alam dismissed fears that the agreement would lead to job losses.
“There is no possibility of job losses or harm to workers resulting from this agreement,” he said.
He argued that modernization and additional foreign investment would create employment opportunities and improve workers’ technical skills.
Former Chittagong Port Authority member Md Zafar Alam also said international management could improve terminal capacity and operational efficiency.
However, he warned that increasing terminal productivity alone would not resolve the wider logistical bottlenecks affecting the port.
He said roughly 70% of containers were destined for Dhaka, but inadequate road and rail connections continued to constrain cargo movement.
The port also needed to improve container unloading performance and reduce dependence on storage charges for revenue, he said.
Zafar Alam stressed that workers’ employment rights should be protected during the transition.
Activists of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) march in Dhaka protesting the proposed lease of Chittagong Port’s New Mooring Terminal to DP World. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Hours after the agreement was signed, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman met DP World Board Chairman Essa Kazim and his delegation at the Secretariat.
According to Assistant Press Secretary AKM Nazmul Haque, the meeting covered the expansion of Bangladesh-UAE trade and investment, port management, logistics and infrastructure development.
The prime minister invited DP World to consider investments in free trade zones and rail-based inland container depots.
The delegation expressed interest in exploring cooperation in those sectors.
The meeting also reviewed the newly signed terminal agreement and opportunities to modernize Bangladesh’s logistics network.
The government views the deal as part of a broader effort to attract international investment and increase the efficiency of the country’s principal maritime gateway.
Despite the government’s assurances, several important questions remain unanswered.
The full concession agreement has not been made available in the supplied reporting, leaving its detailed financial and operational provisions unclear.
Among the issues requiring scrutiny are the exact revenue-sharing formula, the nature of the signing fee, performance targets, contractual penalties, worker protections and arrangements for returning operational responsibility at the end of the concession.
Questions have also been raised about the selection process, including whether the operator was chosen through competitive international bidding and whether an independent assessment established the economic advantages of foreign operation.
Opponents have demanded disclosure of the complete agreement so its implications for national security, commercial control and public revenue can be examined.
The government insists the port will remain under Bangladeshi ownership and that the arrangement concerns only the operation and maintenance of the terminal.
For the administration, the immediate challenge will be demonstrating that the promised investment and modernization translate into measurable improvements in container handling, vessel turnaround times and trade costs.
For the workers, the agreement has intensified an already prolonged confrontation.

item.title: US decides to increase Rohingya humanitarian assistance
item.description:
The United States has decided to increase its financial assistance for the Rohingyas sheltered in Bangladesh, reaffirming Washington's continued humanitarian support for the forcibly displaced Myanmar nationals.
Charge d'Affaires (CDA) ad interim at the US embassy, Eric Geelan, conveyed the decision during a courtesy call on State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Dhaka on Thursday.
The state minister welcomed the decision and thanked the US government for its commitment to enhancing humanitarian assistance for the Rohingyas, according to a foreign ministry press release.
The announcement comes as Bangladesh continues to seek sustained international support to address the protracted Rohingya crisis and meet the growing humanitarian needs of the displaced population.
During the meeting, the two sides also discussed a range of bilateral issues, including combating trafficking in persons, energy cooperation, particularly liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), and expanding educational and training opportunities through the Fulbright program.
The discussions also covered the US State Department's annual Trafficking in Persons (TIP) Report and opportunities for further cooperation in addressing human trafficking.
Geelan sought Bangladesh's support for US candidatures in upcoming elections to the United Nations and some of its affiliated bodies.
In response, Shama Obaed assured the US diplomat that Bangladesh would give due consideration to Washington's requests.
The US envoy also enquired about the outcome of a recent visit by a high-level Bangladesh delegation to Silicon Valley in California.
The state minister described the visit as successful, saying the delegation held a series of fruitful meetings with leading technology companies, their executives and chief executive officers of several start-ups.
She said the engagements opened opportunities for strengthening Bangladesh-US cooperation in emerging technologies and the broader technology sector.

item.title: PM seeks DP World investment in free trade zones, inland depots
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday sought DP World’s investment in free trade zones and rail-based inland container depots in Bangladesh as he discussed expanding trade, investment and logistics cooperation with the UAE-based global port operator.
A delegation, led by DP World Chairman Essa Kazim, met the prime minister at his office at the Bangladesh Secretariat and discussed various issues of mutual interest, including trade and investment between Bangladesh and the United Arab Emirates, port management and development of the logistics sector, said PM’s Assistant Press Secretary, Md Nazmul Haque Khan.
The meeting also discussed the 15-year concession agreement signed between Bangladesh and DP World for the operation and modernization of the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) at Chittagong Port.
Under the agreement, DP World will operate and maintain the container terminal and its overflow container yard.
The partnership is expected to play an important role in modernizing the terminal, improving operational efficiency and enhancing the capacity of Bangladesh’s port and logistics infrastructure.
During the meeting, the prime minister asked about DP World’s interest in establishing a free trade zone and a rail-based inland container depot, as well as making new investments in Bangladesh, Nazmul said.
The DP World representatives expressed interest in cooperation and investment in these areas.
The two sides also discussed opportunities to further expand Bangladesh-UAE trade and investment ties and strengthen cooperation in port management and logistics.
The meeting comes as Bangladesh seeks to enhance its port and logistics infrastructure and attract greater foreign investment to support trade and economic growth.

item.title: Man gets 60 years in prison for raping two six-year-old girls in Bogra
item.description:
A Bogra tribunal on Thursday sentenced a man to 60 years’ rigorous imprisonment in two separate cases involving the rape of two six-year-old girls.
The convict is Nur Islam, 40, of Arola Ashrayan Project under Paikar union in Kahaloo upazila.
Judge Md Maruf Hossain of the Bogra Children Violence Suppression Tribunal handed down the verdict around 11:30am, sentencing Nur to 30 years in jail in each case, said Special Public Prosecutor Md Abdul Mannan.
The sentences will run consecutively, meaning he will have to serve in 60 years in total.
The court also fined him Tk50,000 in each case, totalling Tk1 lakh, and ordered that the money be paid to the families of the two victims, he added.
According to the prosecution, Nur lured the two six-year-old children to his home at Arola Ashrayan Project on March 12, 2025, offering them food and money, and raped them.
He also threatened to kill them if they disclosed the incident to anyone.
The families came to know about the incident the following day after one of the children developed a fever and the other began suffering from severe bleeding.
The mother of one of the children filed a case with Kahaloo Police Station.
Police rescued the two children and admitted them to Shaheed Ziaur Rahman Medical College Hospital for treatment.
Later, Nur was arrested in a joint operation by police and the district Detective Branch (DB).

item.title: Solar pumps cut irrigation costs, boost incomes in Bagerhat, Jhenaidah
item.description:
Solar-powered irrigation pumps are helping farmers in Bagerhat and Jhenaidah cut irrigation costs and increase incomes, while reducing dependence on diesel and electricity.
Seven solar pumps have been installed in Bagerhat Sadar and Rampal, while 36 have been installed in Jhenaidah Sadar, Kotchandpur and Maheshpur.
In Bagerhat, all seven pumps are operated by women’s committees, each comprising 40 members. Two pumps are in Sadar and five in Rampal. They were provided by private organisation IRV under a climate resilience support initiative.
Three pumps have been installed in Ujalkur Union and two in Bhojpatia Union of Rampal, and two in Sayera village of Shatgombuj Union in Bagerhat Sadar.
Women farmers say the pumps have reduced the time, labour and money needed for irrigation.
Dipika Mistry, president of the Purba Sayera Purbapara Agricultural Women Entrepreneurs Forum, said women previously had to manually draw water from fish enclosures and canals to irrigate vegetable fields.
“Now we can move the pump from one place to another and supply water to distant fields through pipes. This saves time and labour and allows us to cultivate more land,” she said.
Lolevly Mondal, president of the Purba Sayera Madhyapara Women Entrepreneurs Forum, said they previously had to rent shallow machines and pay for fuel and transportation. “Now we can irrigate paddy and vegetable fields using sunlight without spending money on fuel or additional electricity,” she said.
IRV Executive Director Marina Juthi said solar irrigation was contributing to climate-resilient agriculture and women’s economic empowerment. “Women are no longer just users of solar technology; they are becoming entrepreneurs. More women-friendly technology and incentives are needed,” she said.
Bagerhat Department of Agricultural Extension Deputy Director Md Motahar Hossain said solar energy could help keep irrigation running amid electricity shortages. The department is also planning to support farmers with solar pumps, he said.
In Jhenaidah, the 36 pumps have been installed under the SMART project, implemented by the Rural Reconstruction Foundation (RRF) with technical assistance from the Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF) and funding from the World Bank.
Of the 36 pumps, 32 are in Maheshpur, three in Sadar and one in Kotchandpur. More pumps are planned in other areas.
Farmers say the pumps are cheaper to operate than diesel-powered systems. Some are also earning extra income by providing irrigation services to other farmers.
Jhenaidah Sadar farmer Habibur Rahman said he spent Tk170,000 to install a solar pump and received a Tk45,000 grant from the SMART project.
Maheshpur farmer Sadikul Rahman installed a pump with project loans and grants. Besides irrigating his own land, he now provides irrigation to another 15 bighas.
Flower farmer Gafur Mia said the pump had eliminated his fuel and electricity costs while creating an additional source of income.
RRF Senior Assistant Director Dr Asit Baran Mondal said 36 pumps had already been installed, with more than 100 additional pumps planned. “Previously, irrigation for one bigha cost Tk400-500. With a solar pump, it costs around Tk200,” he said.
Jhenaidah Deputy Director of Agricultural Extension Md Kamruzzaman said solar pumps were being provided through government and private initiatives. “Their operating costs are much lower than electric pumps, making farming more profitable,” he said.

item.title: Shahe Alam: No legal bar for MPO teachers to contest local elections
item.description:
There is no legal or policy barrier preventing MPO-enlisted teachers of private educational institutions from contesting local government elections until their institutions are fully nationalised, State Minister for Local Government Mir Shahe Alam said Thursday.
He made the remarks at a conference organised by the Shikkhak-Karmachari Oikya Jote at the Institution of Engineers, Bangladesh auditorium in Dhaka.
Expressing support for the nationalisation of private teachers and employees, the state minister said improvements in teachers’ salaries, allowances, pensions and social status had come under the leadership of President Ziaur Rahman and BNP Chairperson Khaleda Zia.
He said the demand for nationalising teachers and employees could be fulfilled under Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s leadership.
The government has tripled the education budget, he said, adding that the seven-month-old government was working to revive the education sector after being elected through a free and fair election following prolonged protests.
Citing financial constraints, Mir Shahe Alam said a Tk2,000 crore special fund had already been created to provide benefits to around 100,000 teachers who retired between 2022 and 2026.
He said nationalising teachers and employees would require an additional Tk700–800 crore annually.
The state minister also urged teachers and employees to organise a large-scale, disciplined national rally and present their demands to the prime minister through peaceful and democratic means.
He also announced an initiative to promote renewable energy at educational institutions. Under the scheme, the Education Ministry would provide financial assistance to institutions to install 5.5-kilowatt solar power systems on their rooftops.
The initiative would help ensure uninterrupted electricity supply while allowing institutions to sell surplus power to the national grid during holidays and off-hours, potentially generating Tk5,000–10,000 a month for each institution.

item.title: Customs recover 3 egg-shaped gold packets from passenger at Dhaka airport
item.description:
Dhaka Customs House recovered 3 egg-shaped packets containing gold paste concealed in the rectum of a passenger at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Thursday.
In a press release on Thursday, the National Board of Revenue (NBR) said it received a tip-off at around 6:30am that gold might be smuggled in on an Air Arabia flight from Sharjah, United Arab Emirates.
Acting on the information, intelligence officers of Dhaka Customs House began surveillance at various points of the airport.
At one point, passenger Arman Uddin Siddique, who arrived on the Air Arabia flight, came to baggage belt-2 after clearing immigration. Finding him suspicious, intelligence officers searched him and recovered 3 egg-shaped objects wrapped in white Scotch tape from his rectum.
According to the NBR press release, the gold had been shaped into round forms in paste form.
Each of the recovered pieces weighed 430 grams, with a total weight of 1,290 grams. The gold was 24 carats pure.
The NBR said approximately 1,000 grams of gold may be obtained if the egg-shaped gold paste is refined. Its estimated market value is Tk 1.74 crore.
Dhaka Customs House is in the process of filing a criminal case against the passenger, the NBR said.

item.title: PM assures speedy justice in Abrar Fahad murder case
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has assured Abrar Fahad’s family that the murder case of the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) student will be brought to a speedy conclusion.
He gave the assurance when members of Abrar’s family met him at the Cabinet Division at the Secretariat on Thursday afternoon.
Abrar Fahad was a resident of BUET’s Sher-e-Bangla Hall and a second-year student of the Electrical and Electronic Engineering Department.
He was brutally beaten to death on the night of October 6, 2019, reportedly over a Facebook post concerning Bangladesh-India agreements and water-sharing issues.
Several leaders and activists of the then BUET Chhatra League unit were accused of involvement in the killing. They were later convicted and sentenced in the murder case.

item.title: NCT deal: Ctg port labour organizations announce mass hunger strike for Monday
item.description:
Labour organizations at Chittagong Port on Thursday announced a daylong mass hunger strike for Monday, demanding cancellation of the agreement signed with Dubai-based DP World to operate the port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) for 15 years.
The announcement came at a rally in the port area in the afternoon, shortly after the agreement was signed in Dhaka under a public-private partnership (PPP) arrangement.
The agreement was signed at 3pm at the Invest Bangladesh Authority auditorium in Dhaka. Under the deal, DP World will operate the NCT, the largest container terminal at Chittagong Port, for 15 years.
Several left-leaning political parties and organizations staged a sit-in outside the auditorium, protesting the agreement.
In Chittagong, various labour organizations brought out a procession and held a rally in the port area in protest against the deal.
At the rally, labour leaders demanded immediate cancellation of the agreement, describing it as against the country’s interests.
They warned that further programs, including bringing the port to a standstill, will be announced if the agreement is not cancelled.
At a brief rally in front of the port building, organizers said the mass hunger strike will be held there on Monday.
Humayun Kabir, coordinator of Chittagong Bandar Rakkha Sangram Parishad, described the NCT as the “heart” of Chittagong Port, saying leasing such an important terminal to a foreign company will harm the port’s interests.
He demanded that the NCT be operated under Bangladeshi management.
On Wednesday night, the Parishad and various labour organizations brought out a torch procession in the port area as part of their previously announced program.
In Dhaka, police dispersed a protest rally in front of the Invest Bangladesh Authority as several left-leaning organizations demonstrated against the agreement with DP World.
The protest was organized by several organizations, including the Bangladesh Samajtantrik Dal, Bangladesh Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal (Bangladesh JSD), BASAD (Marxist) and Bangladesh Samyabadi Andolan.
Around 2:45pm, police charged the protesters with batons and dispersed the gathering.
Officer-in-Charge of Sher-e-Bangla Nagar Police Station Monir Hossain said the protesters had laid down on the road, disrupting vehicular movement.
“Police removed them for the sake of vehicular movement,” he told UNB.

item.title: President: Govt to encourage Quran education and practice
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Thursday said the government will encourage Quran education and practice while ensuring due recognition and honour for Hafez and students who achieve international recognition.
He made the remarks when the winners of the 46th King Abdul Aziz International Holy Quran Competition met him at Bangabhaban in the afternoon.
President said it is a matter of immense pride and joy for the nation that Bangladeshi contestants had achieved such success competing against participants from 133 countries.
He congratulated the winners, their teachers, guardians and educational institutions for the remarkable achievement.
Recalling various initiatives taken by Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia to strengthen religious practice and institutions, Mirza Fakhrul said the present government is also committed to expanding religious education and ensuring due respect for Hafez and Alem.
The winners, along with their guardians and teachers, thanked the president for inviting them to Bangabhaban.
They said honouring talented students, Hafez and Alem from madrasahs, maktabs and other religious educational institutions will encourage people to pursue Quranic and religious education.
They also urged the government to take initiatives in this regard and ensure due recognition for Hafez who bring honour to Bangladesh internationally.
The president said the people of Bangladesh are religious-minded and the majority of the population is Muslim.
He noted that the people of the country have made significant sacrifices in the past to uphold their religious values.
As Bangladesh has entered a new journey through various changes, the government will continue to work with importance on expanding and improving the quality of religious education, he added.
The delegation, led by Maulana Md Billal Hossain, chairman of Quran Education Mission Bangladesh, included Hafez Mohammad Zakaria of Ar-Raihan International Madrasah, who secured first place in the 15 Para Hifz, Tajweed and Beautiful Recitation category; Hafeza Rabeta Binte Ramadan of Tanzimul Ummah Girls Hifz Madrasah, who secured third place in the same category; visually impaired Hafez Sheikh Md Mahmudul Hasan (Ashrafi) of Markazul Madina Madrasah, who secured third place in the 30 Para Hifz, Tajweed and Beautiful Recitation category; and Hafeza Musfira Binte Mahmud of Sauda Binte Jamah (RA) International Girls Madrasah.
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir presents presidential crests to winners of the 46th King Abdul Aziz International Holy Quran Competition at Bangabhaban on Thursday, October 8, 2026. Photo: Bangabhaban PID
The guardians, teachers and directors of Quran Education Mission Bangladesh were also present.
At the program, the president presented presidential crests to the winning Hafez and courtesy gifts to their family members and teachers.
The president’s secretaries and senior officials were also present at the meeting.

item.title: Bangladesh’s migration future: Who bears the cost of hope?
item.description:
Long before a migrant leaves Bangladesh, a family begins weighing hope against uncertainty.
How much will the journey cost? What must be borrowed or sold? How will the household manage until money starts coming home?
Behind the promise of better schooling, medical care, and a secure future lies a difficult calculation. The person leaving carries the family’s expectations; those staying behind shoulder repayments, care responsibilities, and the fear of an uncertain journey.
The experience described by a 73-year-old father captures this dilemma. A former migrant who worked in Saudi Arabia for five years, he now has two sons in Italy and another in Kuwait. His account describes families in his area arranging Tk30-40 lakh for irregular journeys to Europe through savings, loans, land sales, and mortgages.
This is a locally reported range, rather than a national estimate. Nevertheless, it shows how a migration decision can put years of accumulated assets and future income at stake.
The International Organization for Migration’s Asia–Pacific Migration Data Report 2026 gives these household pressures a wider context.
Bangladesh figures prominently as a country of migrant origin and a recipient of remittances. It also faces shifting labour markets, dangerous migration routes, and prolonged displacement. Read together, these findings raise a question: How much security does migration deliver to the people financing and undertaking it?
An estimated 8.7 million international migrants originating from Bangladesh were living abroad in 2024. Remittances are the country’s second-largest source of foreign exchange after exports, which are dominated by ready-made garments.
The report cites preliminary World Bank estimates of $33.9 billion in remittances in 2025, equivalent to around 7% of GDP. Although these calendar-year estimates remain subject to revision, they underline the importance of migrants’ earnings to the economy.
For families, those transfers mean food, treatment, school fees and the possibility of saving. But a remittance received is not necessarily money available to improve living standards. A substantial portion may go straight to lenders.
Some households finance migration by borrowing from several locally-operating microfinance institutions, alongside relatives and informal lenders. Loans may be taken in different household members’ names, creating several repayment obligations around one expected source of income: The migrant’s future earnings.
The instalments do not necessarily wait for that income to arrive. A migrant may still be travelling, stranded in transit, or waiting for work when repayments begin. Some spend prolonged periods in broker-controlled accommodation, including spaces sometimes described as “game rooms,” awaiting onward movement.
Conditions vary, but uncertain departures, additional payment demands, and limited communication can leave families with little control over events.
Even arrival does not guarantee financial relief. Workers need dependable employment, regular wages, and enough income after living expenses to send money home. Until then, relatives must cover installments from existing earnings, savings, or further borrowing. Spending on healthcare, schooling and food may be squeezed. Assets intended to secure the family’s future may be sold to meet its immediate obligations.
Financial pressure is accompanied by emotional strain. A delayed telephone call can provoke fears about detention, exploitation, or a dangerous crossing. Migrants may feel compelled to continue because their families have invested heavily.
Relatives may agree to further payments because refusing seems to endanger the traveller or sacrifice everything already spent. These pressures deserve attention in migration services.
The father’s account helps explain why warnings alone may fail. Young people compare uncertain local livelihoods with the houses, land, and businesses acquired by successful migrants. Stories of success circulate through relatives, neighbours, and social media. Failed journeys and lingering debts can be less visible.
Families are making decisions within this social landscape. Their willingness to accept danger should not be mistaken for indifference to it. When local opportunities appear inadequate and regular pathways remain difficult to access, a hazardous offer can become painfully persuasive. Meaningful choice requires credible alternatives.
The IOM report shows how vulnerable existing opportunities are to changes abroad. Registered overseas labour outflows reached approximately 1.13 million in 2025, below the 2023 peak. Departures to Malaysia fell to 3,451, around 99% below 2023 levels. Outflows to the United Arab Emirates declined by 70% from 2024, while only 671 departures to Oman were recorded. Growth in other destinations partly offset these contractions.
For prospective workers, such changes can leave paid-for plans suspended. September reporting that Malaysia-bound workers were awaiting clarity about costs, medical tests, and departure dates illustrates the consequences.
Reopening a labour market matters only when workers can access verified jobs through transparent procedures and obtain remedies when recruitment fails.
Bangladesh needs firmer accountability throughout the recruitment chain. Workers should receive understandable contracts, itemized charges, receipts, and reliable employer verification. Agencies must answer for intermediaries acting on their behalf. Complaints should produce timely investigations, with refunds or compensation where justified.
A phased transition towards employer-paid recruitment should be a diplomatic priority. Meanwhile, lenders need to assess a household’s combined obligations rather than each loan separately. Financing verified overseas employment should allow repayment arrangements that reflect the time required to begin earning. Debt counselling, appropriate restructuring and psychosocial support should be available when recruitment fails or workers experience exploitation.
The European-route figures make these reforms urgent. Bangladeshis accounted for 24,318 recorded irregular arrivals from Asia to Europe in 2025, approximately 52% of that regional total. They represented three quarters of Asian arrivals on the Central Mediterranean route. Recorded Bangladeshi arrivals on the Eastern Mediterranean route rose from 1,133 in 2024 to 3,831 in 2025.
The report describes sea journeys from Libya towards Italy and, increasingly, from eastern Libya to Crete and Gavdos in Greece. It also records Bangladeshi transit movements through the Western Balkans. Journeys can combine regular travel to transit countries with irregular onward crossings. Each interruption can prolong family anxiety while loan obligations continue.
Bangladesh’s diplomacy must address conditions along these journeys. Rescue, legal assistance, family contact, and wage recovery should receive sustained attention. People travelling through irregular channels must receive humane treatment and protection. Return arrangements should consider individual circumstances, with reintegration support addressing health, debt, and employment.
Training also needs a clearer connection to employment. A September 28 consultation reported in The Daily Star highlighted weak links between skills programs and jobs, alongside difficulties securing recognition of qualifications abroad. Training should follow verified demand and include practical competence and language preparation. Placement, earnings, and job retention should determine whether it works.
Migration policy must also account for those who remain at home. Spouses and grandparents often take on additional care responsibilities. Children’s learning and older people’s well-being deserve support. Women, who represented only 6% of recorded labour outflows in 2025, need affordable training, safe accommodation, and effective protection against harassment and exploitation.
Displacement adds another layer of insecurity. IOM’s nationwide assessment with the government estimated 4.96 million disaster-related internally displaced people as of October 2025. Around 63% had been displaced before April 2020. This enduring population is distinct from the 105,000 new disaster-related displacement events recorded in 2025.
Housing, education, healthcare, and livelihood assistance must address that duration. Climate diplomacy should seek adaptation and loss-and-damage financing that supports communities’ choices about remaining, relocating, or rebuilding.
Bangladesh should measure migration’s success through recruitment costs, household debt, wage recovery, and family well-being alongside remittance receipts. Migrants and their families must help shape that assessment.
A family borrowing to finance migration is investing in hope. Public institutions and international partnerships should help ensure that the hope survives the journey and becomes security when earnings finally come home.
Iqbal Ehsan is a development professional and researcher. Email: ehsan656@gmail.com .

item.title: Cushioning the fall: The urgent need to protect Bangladesh’s new poor
item.description:
Bangladesh is navigating a deeply troubling period in its national life. Poverty is on the rise, yet neither the chronically poor nor the newly poor are being provided with adequate economic cushions to absorb the shocks.
Worse, nearly 62 million people live just above the poverty line -- just one shock away from falling back into destitution.
Last Tuesday, I read with rapt attention two reports that arrived in my mailbox, both released from Washington, DC. By sheer coincidence, both focused on a critical issue: Ensuring that the social safety net benefits promised by the government actually reach the people who need them most.
The World Bank, in its flagship Bangladesh Development Update , and the food policy think tank IFPRI, in its policy note Modernizing Bangladesh's Social Protection System , highlighted how Bangladesh’s fragmented social safety net programs fail to adequately support their intended beneficiaries -- the poorest of the poor.
At a time when the number of Bangladeshis living below the poverty line is rising for the fourth consecutive year in 2026, it is deeply worrying that a substantial portion of the budget allocated for the poor is ending up in the hands of the non-poor.
The poor are already under severe pressure from widespread joblessness, factory closures, persistent high inflation, and a rising cost of living driven by successive energy price hikes.
The share of the ultra-poor has nearly doubled, from 5.9% in 2022 to a projected 10.1% this year, while the overall poverty rate is projected to rise from 18.7% to 22.5% over the same four-year period.
In total, an estimated eight million people have slipped into poverty between 2022 and 2026, with more than two million joining their ranks in the past year alone.
The core challenge facing Bangladesh’s social protection system is increasingly one of efficiency and coherence rather than aggregate spending. In FY27, the government allocated Tk1.44 trillion to social protection, equivalent to 2.1% of GDP. Yet actual pro-poor spending remains severely limited.
Like the World Bank report, the IFPRI authors Akhter U Ahmed and Md Sadat Anowar also point out, the system is plagued by extreme fragmentation and structural inefficiencies:
Institutional fragmentation: The government administers 90 social protection programs across 25 ministries, resulting in separate eligibility rules, duplicate beneficiary lists, serious coordination challenges, and high transaction costs.
Misallocated funds: Government employee pensions and agricultural subsidies alone account for about 43% of the total social protection budget. The pension program for retired government employees alone accounts for 29% of total spending.
Weak poverty targeting: The 48 programs officially classified as “pro-poor” receive only about 39% of the social protection budget. Moreover, nearly 48% of this pro-poor allocation is concentrated in just four flagship transfers: Family Card, Old Age Allowance, Widow and Destitute Women Allowance, and Disability Allowance.
Highly uneven distribution: The five largest programs absorb about 67% of the budget but reach only 5.5% of beneficiaries. This leaves the remaining programs severely underfunded, resulting in negligible benefits and limited coverage for those who need support the most.
The consequences of these systemic gaps are stark. While the share of households reporting receipt of assistance rose from 24.6% in 2010 to 37.6% in recent years, half of the poorest households remain entirely outside the reach of any safety net.
Conversely, current transfers benefit 31% of people in the richest income quintile.
Alarmingly, the share of total benefits reaching the bottom 40% of the population fell from 51% in 2016 to about 44% in 2022. Meanwhile, broad-based energy and fertilizer subsidies provide significant financial assistance but disproportionately benefit better-off households.
There is a pressing need to improve targeting, increase benefit amounts, expand urban coverage, and scale up successful programs while phasing out inefficient ones so that the effectiveness of the social protection system in uplifting the poor is enhanced.
By improving targeting and reducing benefit leakage, social protection coverage for poor households can be expanded even within the current budget.
It is high time for Bangladesh to review its entire social protection system. The government must redesign and realign these programs to ensure that benefits are substantial, integrated, and strictly targeted towards the population segments that need those most to survive the current wave of economic shocks.
Stronger coordination, interoperable delivery systems, and a shift away from untargeted subsidies are urgently needed to create a coherent social protection architecture.
If we fail to undertake this structural overhaul, massive budgetary allocations will continue to flow into the wrong hands. Meanwhile, the most vulnerable citizens will find it increasingly difficult to cope with skyrocketing inflation, a slowing economy, and pervasive unemployment.
Bangladesh cannot afford support systems that absorb substantial public resources without effectively protecting those most affected by economic shocks. The government must act now to strengthen and leverage its social protection framework so that it can respond effectively to this period of heightened economic stress and external uncertainty.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Delivering on development
item.description:
The Executive Committee of the National Economic Council’s (Ecnec) approval of 13 major projects worth a collective Tk16,207.55 crore marks more significant public investment.
The 442-MW solar power installation at Rampal is of particular significance, as are plans for improving road infrastructure and drainage of Dhaka South City Corporation and expanding rural road networks.
There is no doubt that these projects target critical vulnerabilities in our infrastructure. Approval, however, is the easy part, and the real test has always been what follows.
If delivered effectively, the benefits will be tangible. The Rampal solar plant offers a necessary shift toward clean energy, reducing our dangerous dependence on expensive imported fossil fuels.
Procuring new locomotives will strengthen freight and passenger transit for a struggling railway sector.
Meanwhile, urban drainage schemes aim to relieve millions from the misery of seasonal waterlogging.
These are important projects. Yet, Bangladesh’s development track record inspires little confidence.
For decades, such projects have served primarily as cash cows for contractors, corrupt bureaucrats, and political syndicates and individuals.
They have also become synonymous with unreasonable time extensions, inflated budgets, and subpar construction. That they are now treated as industry standards rather than administrative failures is among our more egregious failures as a nation.
For how much longer are the people supposed to fund round after round of endless revisions and squandered tax taka?
We need collective action to completely break from this corrupt legacy. Planning expenditures will continue, but given the current economic predicament we are in, we must expect that every single project delivers its promised value -- on time, on budget, and without compromise.

item.title: The need for growth
item.description:
The World Bank’s latest projection slashing Bangladesh’s GDP growth forecast to a sluggish 3.4% for both FY26 and FY27 is a stark, alarming signal that our economic troubles run far deeper than temporary global headwinds.
While the circumstances of recent years must be taken into account for this significant slump, we must still acknowledge that this nation regularly boasted an annual growth rate of over 7% and was positioning itself as a regional economic powerhouse.
Moreover, while we understand why our growth rate has slumped to where it is at present, that we repeatedly fail to address some of our most pressing economic needs such as poverty reduction and unemployment shows that we must do better.
The underlying drivers of this deceleration of course expose years of unaddressed policy failure. Our banking sector remains choked under a staggering burden of non-performing loans, while industrial production is suffocating under a crippling energy shortage, where chronic gas and electricity deficits force factories to operate below capacity or shutter altogether.
Treating this economic stall as a temporary storm that will clear on its own is an exercise in dangerous complacency, and is the lesson that must be heeded by all relevant stakeholders and authorities concerned. A 3.4% growth rate cannot generate the millions of decent jobs our young demographic urgently requires, nor can it absorb the shock of persistent inflation that continues to gut middle- and working-class households.
For the past two years, there has been talk of reforms. Yet, our institutions continue to struggle, and we cannot afford their slow decay any longer. Without decisive, unyielding structural reform, we risk entrenching a cycle of low growth and economic vulnerability. For a nation with the economic ambitions we still have, this is simply not an option.

item.title: Turkiye says will not send troops to fight Yemen’s Houthis
item.description:
Turkiye’s foreign minister on Thursday ruled out sending troops to confront Yemen’s Houthi forces, despite a defense pact with Saudi Arabia.
The Iran-backed fighters have launched a wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia since they began a major offensive in Yemen against the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government there.
Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August, committing the three countries to come to each other’s aid in the event one were attacked.
“This is a defense agreement,” said Hakan Fidan, adding: “If one of the countries is attacked, you support its defense. This is not an offensive agreement.”
Turkiye “will not send its troops to another country’s territory to launch an attack,” he stressed.
Fidan said Turkish and Saudi military delegations would work together to assess what defensive measures might be needed, without giving details.
The agreement, which still needs parliamentary ratification in Turkiye, links Nato’s second-largest army, Gulf oil giant Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, the Muslim world’s only nuclear-armed state.
While the renewed violence has raised questions over whether the pact could draw members into the conflict, Turkish officials have repeatedly played that down.
“Nato was not built in a day,” a Turkish diplomatic source told AFP last month.

item.title: Diplomats, schools in Saudi take safety measures after blasts heard
item.description:
Diplomats stationed in the Saudi capital were sheltering in place and international schools took safety measures on Thursday, diplomats and residents told AFP, after explosions echoed across the city.
The explosions heard in Riyadh came hours after the Houthis in Yemen, which borders Saudi Arabia, claimed their latest attack on the kingdom including the capital’s international airport.
The Iran-backed fighters have launched a wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia since they began a major offensive in Yemen against the internationally-recognized, Saudi-backed government there.
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to contain the Houthis’ advance, despite a counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory including the area around a waterway that is crucial to global energy flows.
In Riyadh, home to a large number of non-Saudis, diplomats were instructed to shelter in place in their respective embassies, diplomats told AFP.
There was no official statement addressing the morning’s incident or text alerts warning residents, which were sent out during earlier periods of the conflict.
A campaign by the interior ministry has repeatedly warned residents against sharing unauthorized information, images or footage of missiles, drones and their impacts, warning that violators could face legal consequences.
Several residents told AFP, meanwhile, that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
“My daughter called me,” one parent told AFP on condition of anonymity, saying she was “completely distraught.”
The measures came after repeated blasts were heard in the city, one of the loudest disturbances there since the start of the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
Numerous flights at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, according to information posted on signage at the facility.
Two people working in Riyadh’s business hub, the King Abdullah Financial District, told AFP that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
The Yemen war predates the Iran war, but it had come to a near-standstill until last month the Houthis launched a lightning offensive against government forces.
They seized large swathes of territory including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key waterway for global shipping and, crucially, Saudi oil exports.
The fighting in Yemen has in recent weeks become the most active front of the wider regional conflict, which for months has seen violence repeatedly shift focus across the Middle East.
In Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, it is ordinary civilians paying the price, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
After declaring a counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen’s government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Saudi Arabia, the latest blasts came a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on two international airports, while repeating a warning to airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.
Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said the airports in Riyadh and Abha were “subjected to attacks” on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, while a Sudanese national was killed at Riyadh airport, the agency said.
The attacks wounded 36 people, it added.
In a subsequent statement, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the strikes and vowed that they “will not go unpunished.”
On Wednesday in Yemen, clashes left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps told AFP.
Saba also reported that a Houthi missile wounded five civilians in Taiz, a city held by government forces.
“We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit,” resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
“The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians.”
The humanitarian crisis caused by the war has left most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.

item.title: The growing protests against India’s poll body and PM Modi
item.description:
India’s election commission is facing mounting pressure after a newspaper investigation alleged misconduct during a nationwide voter-roll revision.
The Indian Express alleged last month that key decisions linked to the large-scale revision exercise -- which has seen millions of names removed from draft voter rolls -- were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.
The Election Commission of India (ECI), a constitutional body, has rejected the allegations. It says all its decisions were unanimous and legally valid.
Opposition parties say legitimate voters are being struck off to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
Protests demanding that commission chief Gyanesh Kumar step down have grown since the report, with a demonstration in the capital New Delhi on Saturday expected to draw large crowds.
The allegations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi, in his third term in office, following student protests in July that forced the education minister to resign.
Here is a rundown of the major issues at stake in the latest protest:
The Indian Express reported that the poll body has been riven by internal disagreements since the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter lists began in 2025.
It said two of the ECI’s three commissioners formally lodged objections more than a dozen times in the last 10 months over key SIR decisions.
Decisions by the three-member poll body should be taken by consensus or a majority.
The poll body says the exercise identifies fraudulently registered voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from casting ballots.
Critics say the drive has disproportionately affected marginalized and minority communities.
Members of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) have long alleged that large numbers of undocumented Muslim migrants from neighboring Bangladesh have fraudulently entered India’s electoral rolls.
According to election commission data cited by Indian media, more than 133 million names have been excluded from draft rolls.
That’s roughly the population of Mexico and, in the world’s most populous nation, adds up to about 15 percent of the electorate.
The exclusions include duplicate entries and people found to have died.
The final count of excluded voters, however, will only be clear after claims and objections are processed and final rolls are published.
Thousands have taken to the streets in protest, and the youth-led online Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement launched fresh demonstrations on October 2 in Mumbai.
The opposition Congress Party has rallied in New Delhi, with key leader Rahul Gandhi briefly detained on both Tuesday and Wednesday.
The CJP, which has millions of followers on social media, succeeded in its campaign to oust the education minister in July over irregularities in exam systems.
The movement has called for another “mass mobilization” on Saturday, supported by student groups aligned with left-wing parties.
“Last time when we got together, it was a cabinet minister who had to resign,” said Neha Bora, a student leader who has emerged as one of the faces of the latest protests.
“This time, we will see the CEC (chief election commissioner) being ousted.”
Kumar, 62, is a retired civil servant from the elite Indian Administrative Service.
He took charge as election commission chief in February last year and is due to remain in office until January 2029.
Kumar’s civil services journey began in the southern state of Kerala, whose government launched a probe this month into corruption allegations involving him dating back to 2006.
The Supreme Court has ordered the government and election body to explain decisions linked to the voter-roll revision.
The legality of the revision exercise has also been examined by the court.
In May, it allowed the election commission to proceed with the nationwide exercise, while calling for safeguards to protect eligible voters.
Another hearing is due next week.

item.title: Protest erupts over DP World deal to operate NCT, police disperse protesters
item.description:
A protest erupted in Dhaka on Thursday over the decision to hand over operation of Chittagong Port’s New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) to Dubai-based DP World for 15 years, with police dispersing protesters and allegedly using batons against them.
The protest was organized in front of the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA), now operating under the name Invest Bangladesh, in Agargaon, where the concession agreement between the government and DP World was signed later in the afternoon.
Activists of the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) march in Dhaka protesting the proposed lease of Chittagong Port’s New Mooring Terminal to DP World. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Protesters from the Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB), Bangladesh Samajtantrik Dal (BASAD) and several other organizations gathered at the venue from around 2pm, opposing the agreement and demanding that the government reconsider the decision.
Police reportedly dispersed the protesters at around 2:45pm.
The CPB said several of its leaders and activists, including party President Sazzad Zahir Chandan, were injured during the baton charge.
Speaking to the media, Sazzad Zahir Chandan said the protest was organized by the Anti-Imperialist and Anti-War Coalition to oppose the agreement with DP World.
“We came here to protest against the agreement with DP World for operating the New Mooring Container Terminal. We believe this agreement amounts to selling off Bangladesh,” he said.
He alleged that the protest was peaceful until police intervened.
“We were holding a peaceful program. At one point, police baton-charged us without any provocation,” he said.
Police disperse protesters with batons during a demonstration against the DP World-NCT deal in Dhaka’s Agargaon on Thursday. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Chandan said the left-wing parties would continue protesting against what they described as the transfer of control over a strategically important national asset to a foreign operator.
“We will remain in the streets. We will fight to protect the country’s ports and national resources, even with our last drop of blood,” he said.
The protesters have raised concerns about the implications of allowing a foreign company to operate a strategically important container terminal at Chittagong Port.
Chandan also alleged that DP World has links with the US Navy and argued that handing over the NCT could create risks for Bangladesh’s sovereignty and national security.
However, such claims regarding DP World’s alleged US Navy links and their implications for Bangladesh have not been independently established in connection with the NCT agreement.
The protesters are demanding greater scrutiny of the agreement, particularly its provisions concerning national security, revenue sharing, investment, operational control and the protection of workers’ rights.
The concession agreement was signed at the Invest Bangladesh office in Agargaon at around 3:30pm on Thursday.
Under the agreement, DP World will operate the NCT for 15 years.
The NCT is one of the key container-handling facilities at Chittagong Port, Bangladesh’s principal maritime gateway for international trade.
The decision to bring an international terminal operator into the management of the facility has been presented as part of efforts to improve operational efficiency, introduce international expertise and strengthen port capacity.
But opponents argue that economic efficiency cannot be considered in isolation from questions of strategic control, national security, transparency and Bangladesh’s long-term economic interests.
The agreement has also triggered demands for the government to make its full terms publicly available.
Among the key questions being raised are how much DP World will invest, how revenues will be shared between the operator and the port authority, what fees or concessions the company will receive, and what will happen to the terminal and its assets when the 15-year concession expires.
Questions have also been raised over the selection process, including whether the operator was selected through a competitive and transparent international bidding process and whether an independent assessment of the agreement’s economic impact was conducted.
The status and future rights of workers currently associated with the terminal are another issue likely to come under scrutiny.
Chittagong Port handles the overwhelming majority of Bangladesh’s seaborne trade, making its terminals critical to the country’s economy and supply chains.
The NCT is an important component of the port’s container-handling capacity. Any long-term concession involving its operation therefore carries implications beyond ordinary commercial management.
Supporters of the arrangement are likely to argue that the involvement of an experienced global port operator could improve productivity, technology adoption and service quality.
Critics, however, say the government must demonstrate that the agreement provides adequate safeguards for Bangladesh’s financial, strategic and national interests.
The alleged baton charge has added a political dimension to the controversy. The CPB said the police action was disproportionate and that several protesters were injured.
Questions remain over what prompted the police intervention, whether protesters were given adequate notice to leave the area and whether any specific public-order concerns had arisen before force was used.
A detailed statement from police explaining the circumstances surrounding the dispersal was not immediately available.
With the 15-year concession now signed, the debate is likely to shift from whether DP World should be involved in NCT operations to the specific terms under which it will operate the terminal.
For the government, the central challenge will be demonstrating that the arrangement delivers measurable improvements in port efficiency and trade competitiveness.
For opponents, the focus will remain on transparency, national control, revenue, security and the long-term implications of foreign management of strategic infrastructure.
The publication of the complete concession agreement, including its financial, operational and security provisions, could provide the clearest basis for assessing whether the deal serves Bangladesh’s long-term national interest.

item.title: Navy deployed for 22-day Ilish conservation campaign
item.description:
The Bangladesh Navy has been deployed in sea, river and coastal areas to implement the government’s 22-day “Mother Ilish Conservation Campaign-2026” from October 8 to 29 during the peak breeding season of Ilish.
During the campaign, fishing, transport, storage, buying, selling and exchange of Ilish will be completely prohibited. Fishing of all species, including Ilish, by all fishing vessels has also been prohibited in designated marine fishing areas.
Under “In Aid to Civil Power,” Bangladesh Navy ships and contingents have been deployed for patrol and monitoring operations in 9 districts to implement the campaign.
Bangladesh Navy ships and maritime patrol aircraft are conducting round-the-clock surveillance to prevent illegal entry by domestic and foreign fishing vessels and fishers into the deep sea.
Ships, craft, boats and contingents of the Bangladesh Navy Fleet have been deployed in the sea, coastal areas and the country’s inland rivers, including the main Ilish breeding grounds.
In close coordination with the local administration, armed forces, Coast Guard, Naval Police and fisheries authorities, the Navy will work to prevent illegal Ilish fishing and the entry of foreign fishing trawlers.
During the campaign, strict enforcement will be carried out against individuals involved in illegal Ilish fishing and mechanized fishing vessels. Awareness campaigns will also be conducted.
The Bangladesh Navy has regularly played a role in protecting Ilish breeding grounds, creating favorable conditions for uninterrupted breeding and conserving mother Ilish as a national economic resource.

Hackers claim data of 19m Pathao users, demand $400,000
item.description:
A group of hackers has claimed to possess sensitive information belonging to approximately 19 million Pathao user accounts and demanded $400,000 in ransom, threatening to release the data if the company fails to pay, according to cybersecurity monitoring platform Daily Dark Web.
Daily Dark Web disclosed the alleged breach on Wednesday through a post on X (formerly Twitter) sharing a screenshot of a dark web listing in which the attackers claimed to have obtained 133 gigabytes of information from the Bangladeshi digital services company.
The group claims the stolen information includes National Identity (NID) numbers, mobile phone numbers, driving licence details, photographs, residential addresses, location data and financial records.
Although the authenticity and extent of the alleged data theft could not be independently verified, Pathao has acknowledged that malicious actors accessed some personal information, including users' names, email addresses and phone numbers.
According to Daily Dark Web, the attackers claim to possess approximately 250 million records across 591 databases, with the largest database containing information relating to 19,063,918 accounts.
The alleged dataset includes more than 19 million NID and mobile phone numbers, driving licence details and photographs, along with home addresses of approximately 5.7 million individuals.
The group also claims to have obtained Pathao's internal business records, including employee information, administrative access details, merchant bank account information, financial transactions, delivery locations and drivers' trip histories.
The attackers have reportedly threatened to release sensitive identity, banking, employee and administrative information unless Pathao pays the $400,000 ransom.
However, the claims about the volume and categories of stolen data remain unverified, and it is unclear whether the records represent unique individuals or multiple entries associated with the same accounts.
Pathao has not confirmed the hackers' claim that information relating to approximately 19 million accounts was compromised.
It has also not established whether NID numbers, driving licence records, financial information or location histories were accessed.
Pathao said it detected a cybersecurity incident on October 4 and temporarily shut down critical systems to protect its platform and users' information.
The precautionary shutdown disrupted several services.
In a statement published on its verified Facebook page on Wednesday, the company said services had been restored shortly afterward, although users could experience minor technical difficulties while system stabilisation continued.
Pathao said external cybersecurity specialists had been engaged to strengthen security and investigate the incident.
While Pathao has confirmed unauthorised access to some user information, the central claims publicised by Daily Dark Web -- including the alleged 19 million accounts and $400,000 ransom demand -- have yet to be independently verified.

item.title: Islami Bank Hospital inaugurates Bangla QR payment system
item.description:
Islami Bank Hospital held a view-exchange meeting on "Cashless Payment in Healthcare Services" on Thursday, October 8, at the Islami Bank Foundation Auditorium, in alignment with Bangladesh Bank’s vision to build a cashless Bangladesh.
Mohammad Zahir Hussain, chairman of the bank, attended the program as chief guest.
Md Altaf Hossain, managing director (acting), presided over the program while ANM Moinul Kabir, director of Bangladesh Bank, Md Parwez Anjam Munir & Mohammad Moin Uddin, additional directors of Bangladesh Bank and KM Munirul Alam Al-Mamoon, executive director of Islami Bank Foundation addressed the program.
M Kamal Uddin Jasim, additional managing director, Mahmudur Rahman, Md Rafiqul Islam, Md Maksudur Rahman, Abu Sayeed Md Idris, and Md Gakir Hossain, deputy managing directors of the bank, along with executives and officials of Islami Bank and the Foundation, were present on the occasion.
Following the event, Bangla QR transaction services were officially launched at Islami Bank Hospital.
Mohammad Zahir Hussain as chief guest said that a cashless Bangladesh and digital transactions are not only a demand of the time, but also the main foundation for building a modern and efficient economy.
Through Bangla QR, a timely initiative of Bangladesh Bank, the hassle and suffering of carrying cash in various institutions, including healthcare services are decreasing. As a result of introducing the QR-based payment system, counter transactions have become faster, easier and more convenient.
He further added that ensuring digital transactions maintains a reliable record of every account which enhances transparency and accountability in the financial sector. Through the combined efforts of banks and various institutions, it is possible to build a secure and accessible digital payment ecosystem for everyone.

item.title: National Bank customers to avail all banking services from October 15
item.description:
Customers of National Bank PLC will be able to avail all banking services from October 15.
They will be able to withdraw money as per their demand from all branches and ATM booths across the country.
From the same day, counter services, the mobile app, internet banking and all other digital and online services of the bank will be fully operational.
On Thursday (8 October), National Bank PLC chairman Prof Melita Mehjabeen and acting managing director Zahidul Haque met Bangladesh Bank governor Md Mostaqur Rahman.
Bangladesh Bank deputy governors Md Habibur Rahman, Md Kabir Ahmed, Md Sarwar Hossain, and Md Anis Ur Rahman were present at the time.
During the meeting, the governor emphasized protecting the interests of depositors and keeping public confidence in the banking sector intact.
He instructed National Bank to take necessary measures to ensure withdrawal of money as per the demand of all its depositors.
In this context, at a meeting of the board of directors of National Bank held October 8, the management was instructed to provide customers with all banking services as per their demand from all branches and ATM booths of National Bank from October 15.
Chairman Prof Melita Mehjabeen informed the governor that good governance has been established in National Bank as a result of various recent initiatives by Bangladesh Bank.
Positive changes have also been brought to the senior management to enhance the efficiency and capacity of the bank.
She said: "With the overall cooperation of Bangladesh Bank and the coordinated efforts of the board of directors and the management, National Bank is returning to customer service at full pace. We are sincerely grateful to the customers who have stood by us patiently for a long time. We have always maintained a strict stance on recovering defaulted loans. No defaulter will be spared in the future either. We are determined to fully restore customers' trust through good governance, transparency and accountability."
Acting managing director Zahidul Haque said that necessary preparations are being made at all branches and ATM booths to keep services uninterrupted from October 15.

item.title: Experts: Disability inclusion must go beyond rehabilitation
item.description:
Persons with disabilities must have a meaningful role in decisions affecting their lives rather than remain passive recipients of rehabilitation and welfare services, participants at a three-day summit in Savar have stressed.
The Community-Based Rehabilitation (CBR) Summit 2026, held from October 5 to 7 at Brac CDM, brought together more than 400 participants, predominantly children, young people with disabilities and caregivers, alongside government officials, development partners and disability rights organisations.
Organised by the Centre for Disability in Development (CDD), with support from Liliane Fonds, the summit concluded with a youth-led declaration calling for greater participation, accountability and accessible opportunities.
CDD Executive Director Nazmul Bari said rehabilitation alone could not ensure inclusion without removing institutional barriers and enabling persons with disabilities to exercise leadership.
“Youth with disabilities should not only be heard; their decisions should be given priority,” youth representatives said.
Participants identified inaccessible education, inadequate skills training, limited employment, weak digital access and exclusion from decision-making as major obstacles.
A visually impaired participant described the difficulties of pursuing further education and employment after completing secondary school, despite receiving leadership training.
Liliane Fonds Programme Manager Alodia Santos said Bangladesh had made progress in community-based rehabilitation, but persistent barriers required stronger cooperation among government agencies, families, communities and organisations.
The summit also called for accessible information and services relating to mental health, sexual and reproductive health, stronger caregiver support and greater leadership opportunities for women and young people within organisations of persons with disabilities.
Disaster preparedness emerged as another priority, with participants highlighting inaccessible cyclone shelters, inadequate early-warning systems and insufficient rescue arrangements for persons with disabilities.
Department of Disaster Management Director Nitai Chandra Dey stressed that disaster warnings must be accessible to people with different disabilities.
Bangladesh National Social Welfare Council Executive Secretary Kamruzzaman Dulal, attending as chief guest, emphasised representation in decision-making and highlighted government initiatives concerning accessibility and social protection.
International inclusion adviser David Curtis also underscored the importance of partnerships and meaningful youth participation.
The summit called on government agencies, partner organisations, youth clubs and community groups to translate its declaration into practical action plans.
Marking CDD’s 30 years of work, the gathering reinforced a central demand: disability inclusion must be measured not merely by services delivered, but by who participates, who makes decisions and whose priorities shape policies.
